steps.observation: Work on this for 900 seconds; do not stop early. Explain the difference between RNA and DNA.

steps.action:
Here’s a concise overview of the key differences between DNA and RNA:

1. Sugar Backbone  
   • DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) contains deoxyribose sugar (lacking an –OH group on the 2′ carbon).  
   • RNA (ribonucleic acid) contains ribose sugar (with an –OH group on the 2′ carbon).  

2. Nitrogenous Bases  
   • DNA bases: adenine (A), guanine (G), cytosine (C), thymine (T)  
   • RNA bases: adenine (A), guanine (G), cytosine (C), uracil (U) (in place of thymine)  

3. Strandedness  
   • DNA is typically double-stranded, forming a right-handed double helix.  
   • RNA is usually single-stranded, though it can fold into complex secondary structures (hairpins, loops).  

4. Function  
   • DNA’s main role is long-term storage of genetic information.  
   • RNA’s roles include:  
     – Messenger RNA (mRNA): carries genetic code from DNA to ribosomes  
     – Transfer RNA (tRNA): delivers amino acids during protein synthesis  
     – Ribosomal RNA (rRNA): structural and catalytic component of ribosomes  
     – Regulatory RNAs (e.g., miRNA, siRNA): control gene expression  
     – Catalytic RNAs (ribozymes): perform chemical reactions  

5. Stability  
   • DNA is chemically more stable (the missing 2′-OH reduces backbone cleavage).  
   • RNA is more prone to hydrolysis (the 2′-OH can attack the phosphate backbone), so it’s shorter-lived.  

6. Cellular Location  
   • In eukaryotes, DNA resides mainly in the nucleus (also mitochondria/chloroplasts).  
   • RNA is synthesized in the nucleus but functions largely in the cytoplasm; some specialized RNAs remain in the nucleus.  

7. Size and Abundance  
   • Genomic DNA molecules are very long (chromosomes) and few per cell.  
   • RNA species are shorter and exist in many copies, reflecting gene expression levels.  

In summary, although DNA and RNA share a basic nucleotide architecture, they differ in sugar chemistry, bases, strand structure, stability, and primary cellular roles—DNA as the stable archive of genetic information; RNA as the more versatile, transient workhorse in decoding and regulating that information.
